pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the Korean words for 'win' and 'lose,' which are antonyms used in competitions or games. '이기다' means to win or be victorious, and '지다' means to lose or be defeated. These words are commonly used in sports, games, and other competitive situations.

examples.english: Our team won the game.
I lost in soccer.
I want to win the competition.

pages.title: Young vs Old (age)
pages.description: This chart shows the opposite words for age in Korean: young and old. '어리다' means to be young, and '늙다' means to be old. These words help describe how old so…
pages.imageAlt: Young vs Old (age) in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: People can be very different by age. 🔴 어리다 [eorida] - Young
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the opposite words for age in Korean: young and old. '어리다' means to be young, and '늙다' means to be old. These words help describe how old someone or something is. Learning these antonyms is useful for talking about people or animals at different ages.

examples.korean: 나는 어릴 때 친구들과 많이 놀았어요.
examples.english: I played a lot with friends when I was young.
Grandfather has gotten very old.
Puppies are really cute when they are young.

pages.title: This vs that feel in Korean
pages.titleEn: This vs that feel in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, words like 이것, 그것, and 저것 are used to point out things based on their location. 이것 means 'this' for something near the speaker, 그것 means 'that' fo…
pages.imageAlt: This vs that feel in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused about "this," "that," and "that over there" in Korean? 🔴 이것 [igeot] - this (near me)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, words like 이것, 그것, and 저것 are used to point out things based on their location. 이것 means 'this' for something near the speaker, 그것 means 'that' for something near the listener, and 저것 means 'that' for something far from both. 어느 것 means 'which one?' and is used when asking to choose between options.

examples.english: This is my book.
That is your bag.
What is that over there?

pages.title: Already vs yet in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 이미 and 벌써 both mean "already," but 벌써 is used when something happened sooner than expected or with surprise. 아직 means "not yet," indicating someth…
pages.imageAlt: Already vs yet in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused about "already" vs "yet" in Korean? 🔴 이미 [imi] - already (fact)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 이미 and 벌써 both mean "already," but 벌써 is used when something happened sooner than expected or with surprise. 아직 means "not yet," indicating something has not happened up to now. 아직도 means "still," showing that something continues to happen or remain the same. These words help express time and expectations clearly in daily conversations.

examples.english: I already did my homework.
Did you already have dinner? (with surprise)
I haven't done my homework yet.

pages.title: Asking politely in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows polite ways to ask questions in Korean. These expressions are commonly used to ask for information or help politely. They are useful for beg…
pages.imageAlt: Asking politely in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for asking politely ✨ 🔴 있어요? [isseoyo?] - Do you have…?
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows polite ways to ask questions in Korean. These expressions are commonly used to ask for information or help politely. They are useful for beginners who want to speak respectfully in everyday situations.

examples.english: Do you have a book?
Can you do this for me?
Where is the bathroom?

pages.title: Because & so in Korean
pages.description: Because and so are common connectors in Korean used to explain reasons and results. 왜냐하면 means "because" and introduces a reason. 그래서 and 그러니까 both mean "so"…
pages.imageAlt: Because & so in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Learn how to connect ideas in Korean with these handy words 👇 🔴 왜냐하면 [waenyahamyeon] - because
pages.explanationEn: Because and so are common connectors in Korean used to explain reasons and results. 왜냐하면 means "because" and introduces a reason. 그래서 and 그러니까 both mean "so" or "therefore" and show the result or conclusion. 그래서요 is a casual way to say "that's why" in conversation.

examples.english: It is raining. So, I am staying at home.
Because I was hungry, I ate food.
I'm late. So, I have to go quickly.

pages.title: Become / change in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows Korean verbs related to becoming or changing. '되다' means to become or to turn into something. '바꾸다' is used when you change something else,…
pages.imageAlt: Become / change in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to say "become" and "change" in Korean? 🔴 되다 [doeda] - to become
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows Korean verbs related to becoming or changing. '되다' means to become or to turn into something. '바꾸다' is used when you change something else, like an object or a plan. '변하다' describes a change in yourself or something's state. These verbs help you talk about changes in everyday life.

examples.english: I want to become a doctor.
I changed the color of my clothes.
The weather has changed a lot.

pages.title: Before vs after in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 'before' and 'after' are used to talk about when something happens in relation to another event. '전에' means 'before' and is used after a noun or v…
pages.imageAlt: Before vs after in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to say BEFORE and AFTER in Korean? Use these when you talk about time! 👇 🔴 수업 전에 [sueop jeone] - before class
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'before' and 'after' are used to talk about when something happens in relation to another event. '전에' means 'before' and is used after a noun or verb to show something happens earlier. '후에' means 'after' and is used similarly to show something happens later. These expressions help describe time order clearly.

examples.english: I do my homework before class.
I meet my friend after class.
Please wash your hands before eating.

pages.title: Can vs may nuance in Korean
pages.titleEn: Can vs may nuance in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 'can' and 'may' express ability and permission, but they have different nuances. '할 수 있어요' shows you have the ability to do something. '해도 돼요' mea…
pages.imageAlt: Can vs may nuance in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Can vs May in Korean? Here's the quick difference: 🔴 할 수 있어요 [hal su isseoyo] - I can do it (ability)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'can' and 'may' express ability and permission, but they have different nuances. '할 수 있어요' shows you have the ability to do something. '해도 돼요' means you have permission to do it. Negative forms like '못 해요' and '하면 안 돼요' express inability and prohibition, respectively.

examples.english: I can speak Korean.
May I take pictures here?
You shouldn't use your phone now.

pages.title: Counters for people and things
pages.titleEn: Counters for people and things in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, different counters are used to count people, animals, books, and general objects. For example, '명' is used for people, '마리' for animals, '권' for b…
pages.imageAlt: Counters for people and things in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Counting two? Use different words depending on what you count 👇 🔴 두 명 [du myeong] - two people
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, different counters are used to count people, animals, books, and general objects. For example, '명' is used for people, '마리' for animals, '권' for books, and '개' for things. These counters come after numbers to specify what you are counting. Learning these counters helps you speak more naturally and clearly in Korean.

examples.english: Two friends went to school.
I bought two apples.

examples.korean: 강아지 두 마리가 공원에서 놀고 있어요.
examples.english: Two puppies are playing in the park.

pages.title: This that these those in Korean
pages.titleEn: This that these those in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, demonstratives like 이것, 그것, 저것, and 이것들 help you point to things based on their location. 이것 means 'this' for something close to the speaker. 그것 m…
pages.imageAlt: This that these those in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Learn how to say this, that, and those in Korean — super useful for pointing things out! 👇 🔴 이것 [igeot] - this
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, demonstratives like 이것, 그것, 저것, and 이것들 help you point to things based on their location. 이것 means 'this' for something close to the speaker. 그것 means 'that' for something near the listener. 저것 refers to 'that' over there, far from both. 이것들 is the plural form of 이것, meaning 'these'.

examples.english: This is my book.
That is your bag.
Those over there are mountains.

pages.title: Early vs late arrival
pages.titleEn: Early vs late arrival in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows words used to talk about arriving early, on time, or late in Korean. You can use these words to describe when someone gets somewhere compare…
pages.imageAlt: Early vs late arrival in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Arriving early or late? Here’s what you can say on the subway 👇 🔴 일찍 [iljjik] - early
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows words used to talk about arriving early, on time, or late in Korean. You can use these words to describe when someone gets somewhere compared to the expected time. It helps you understand how to talk about time and punctuality in everyday situations.

examples.english: I always go to school early.
The bus arrived on time.
I was too late for the meeting. I'm sorry.

pages.title: Give vs receive in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows the basic Korean verbs for giving and receiving. '주다' means 'to give,' and '받다' means 'to receive.' You can use polite forms like '주세요' to a…
pages.imageAlt: Give vs receive in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Giving and receiving gifts in Korean 🎁 🔴 주다 [juda] - to give
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the basic Korean verbs for giving and receiving. '주다' means 'to give,' and '받다' means 'to receive.' You can use polite forms like '주세요' to ask someone to give you something, and past tense like '받았어요' to say you received something. These verbs are essential for everyday conversations in Korean.

examples.english: Please give me the book.
I received a gift.
My friend gave me food.

pages.title: Hope & wish in Korean
pages.description: These Korean expressions are used to talk about hopes and wishes. 으면 좋겠어요 is used when you hope something will happen. 고 싶어요 expresses a personal desire or w…
pages.imageAlt: Hope & wish in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Want to express hope or wish in Korean? 🔴 으면 좋겠어요 [eumyeon jokesseoyo] - I hope
pages.explanationEn: These Korean expressions are used to talk about hopes and wishes. 으면 좋겠어요 is used when you hope something will happen. 고 싶어요 expresses a personal desire or wish to do something. 바라요 is a polite way to say hope or wish, often for others. 됐으면 is used to ask or hope for something to be allowed or to happen.

examples.english: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
I wish to learn Korean.
I hope everyone stays healthy.

pages.title: Hungry vs full scenes
pages.titleEn: Hungry vs full scenes in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean expressions to talk about feeling hungry, full, or thirsty. You can use these phrases to describe your body’s needs or wants.…
pages.imageAlt: Hungry vs full scenes in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Feeling hungry or full? Know how to say it right in Korean! 🔴 배고파요 [baegopayo] - I'm hungry
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean expressions to talk about feeling hungry, full, or thirsty. You can use these phrases to describe your body’s needs or wants. It also includes a simple sentence to express wanting a snack. These are useful for beginners to talk about everyday feelings related to food and drink.

examples.english: I am hungry. I want to eat rice.
I want a snack. I am thirsty.
I am full. I can't eat anymore.

pages.title: Indefinite pronouns in Korean
pages.description: Indefinite pronouns in Korean are words used to refer to people in a general or unknown way. They include words like 'everybody,' 'somebody,' 'anybody,' and…
pages.imageAlt: Indefinite pronouns in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Need to talk about people without naming them? 🔴 모두 [modu] - everybody
pages.explanationEn: Indefinite pronouns in Korean are words used to refer to people in a general or unknown way. They include words like 'everybody,' 'somebody,' 'anybody,' and 'nobody.' These pronouns help talk about people without specifying exactly who they are. They are useful in everyday conversation when the exact person is not important or unknown.

examples.english: Everybody went to school.
Somebody is at the door.
Nobody knows that story.

pages.title: Invite & soft refuse
pages.description: This chart shows common phrases used to invite someone and politely refuse in Korean. You can use these expressions to ask if someone wants to join an activi…
pages.imageAlt: Invite & soft refuse in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Handy Korean for invite & soft refuse ✨ 🔴 올래요? [ollaeyo?] - Want to come?
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common phrases used to invite someone and politely refuse in Korean. You can use these expressions to ask if someone wants to join an activity and respond kindly if you cannot. These phrases are simple and useful for beginners learning everyday conversation.

examples.english: Friend, do you want to come watch a movie?
Sure! Let's go together.
I can't today. Maybe next time.

pages.title: Know-how expressions in Korean
pages.description: These Korean expressions are used to talk about knowing something or knowing how to do something. '알아요' means 'I know,' and '몰라요' means 'I don't know.' To sa…
pages.imageAlt: Know-how expressions in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you want to say you know something or a skill in Korean, use these handy phrases 👇 🔴 알아요 [arayo] - I know
pages.explanationEn: These Korean expressions are used to talk about knowing something or knowing how to do something. '알아요' means 'I know,' and '몰라요' means 'I don't know.' To say you know how to do something, use '할 줄 알아요.' When you want to say you have learned something, use '배웠어요.' These phrases are common in everyday conversations.

examples.english: I know Korean.
I don't know this problem.
I know how to play the piano.

pages.title: Lend vs borrow scenes
pages.titleEn: Lend vs borrow scenes in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows the difference between 'lend' and 'borrow' in Korean. '빌리다' means to borrow something from someone. '빌려주다' means to lend something to someon…
pages.imageAlt: Lend vs borrow scenes in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When you need something for a short time: 🔴 빌리다 [billida] - borrow
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows the difference between 'lend' and 'borrow' in Korean. '빌리다' means to borrow something from someone. '빌려주다' means to lend something to someone. When you give something back, you use '돌려주다'. '잠깐 쓸게' is a casual phrase to say you will keep something for a short time.

examples.english: Can I borrow the book?
I will lend you a pencil.
I will return the book tomorrow.

pages.title: Like / prefer / love scenes
pages.titleEn: Like / prefer / love scenes in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows how to express different levels of liking or loving something in Korean. You can say 좋아해요 to mean 'like,' 더 좋아해요 to say 'prefer,' 사랑해요 to ex…
pages.imageAlt: Like / prefer / love scenes in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How do you say your feelings in Korean? 🔴 좋아해요 [joahaeyo] - like
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows how to express different levels of liking or loving something in Korean. You can say 좋아해요 to mean 'like,' 더 좋아해요 to say 'prefer,' 사랑해요 to express 'love,' and 안 좋아해요 to say 'don't like.' These words help you talk about your feelings or choices clearly.

examples.english: I like coffee.
I prefer coffee to tea.
I love my family.

pages.title: Listen vs hear scenes
pages.titleEn: Listen vs hear scenes in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 듣다 means to listen actively, focusing on sounds or speech. 들리다 means to hear something that is audible, often without trying. 우연히 듣다 means to over…
pages.imageAlt: Listen vs hear scenes in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Listen vs Hear in real life 👂 🔴 듣다 [deutda] - actively listen
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 듣다 means to listen actively, focusing on sounds or speech. 들리다 means to hear something that is audible, often without trying. 우연히 듣다 means to overhear by chance, and 못 들은 척 means to pretend not to hear or ignore sounds. These words help describe different ways of perceiving sound in everyday situations.

examples.english: I am listening to music.
I can hear children laughing outside.

examples.korean: 그는 내 이야기를 못 들은 척했어요.
examples.english: He pretended not to hear my story.

pages.title: Location particles in Korean
pages.description: Location particles in Korean show where an action happens or the direction of movement. '에' indicates a destination or place where something exists. '에서' is…
pages.imageAlt: Location particles in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Where do you go? Where are you? How do you get there? 🤔 🔴 에 [e] - to / at (destination)
pages.explanationEn: Location particles in Korean show where an action happens or the direction of movement. '에' indicates a destination or place where something exists. '에서' is used to show the place where an action takes place. '으로' points to a direction or means by which something is done. '부터' marks the starting point in time or place.

examples.english: I go to school.
I study at the library.
I came home by bus.

pages.title: More & most in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows words used to compare amounts or degrees in Korean. '더' means 'more,' and '가장' means 'the most.' '덜' means 'less,' and '만큼' means 'as much a…
pages.imageAlt: More & most in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Want to say "more" or "the most" in Korean? 🔴 더 [deo] - more
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows words used to compare amounts or degrees in Korean. '더' means 'more,' and '가장' means 'the most.' '덜' means 'less,' and '만큼' means 'as much as.' These words help you talk about differences or similarities between things in everyday conversation.

examples.english: I study more than my friend.
This bag is the most beautiful.
Today is less cold than yesterday.

pages.title: Must vs should in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 'must' and 'should' express different levels of obligation or advice. '해야 해요' means you have to do something, showing a strong necessity. '하는 게 좋아…
pages.imageAlt: Must vs should in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: When to use must vs should in Korean? 🔴 해야 해요 [haeya haeyo] - must / have to
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 'must' and 'should' express different levels of obligation or advice. '해야 해요' means you have to do something, showing a strong necessity. '하는 게 좋아요' suggests that it is better or advisable to do something, but it is not mandatory. There are also expressions like '안 해도 돼요' meaning you don't have to do something, and '하는 편이 좋아요' which means it is better to do something, often used for polite advice.

examples.english: You must do your homework.
You should exercise.
You don't have to do it today.

pages.title: Open/close vs on/off
pages.description: In Korean, 열다 and 닫다 are used to talk about opening and closing things like doors or windows. 켜다 and 끄다 are used to turn on and off devices like lights or el…
pages.imageAlt: Open/close vs on/off in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Open and close vs on and off 🚪 열다 [yeolda] - open the door
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 열다 and 닫다 are used to talk about opening and closing things like doors or windows. 켜다 and 끄다 are used to turn on and off devices like lights or electronics. These pairs help you describe everyday actions clearly. Remember, 열다/닫다 is for opening and closing physical objects, while 켜다/끄다 is for switching devices on or off.

examples.english: I opened the door and entered the room.
Please turn on the light.
I closed the window and turned off the light.

pages.title: Polite vs casual endings in Korean
pages.titleEn: Polite vs casual endings in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, polite and casual endings show different levels of respect when speaking. Polite endings are used with strangers, elders, or in formal situations.…
pages.imageAlt: Polite vs casual endings in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to be polite or casual in Korean greetings & thanks👇 🔴 안녕하세요 [annyeonghaseyo] - polite hello
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, polite and casual endings show different levels of respect when speaking. Polite endings are used with strangers, elders, or in formal situations. Casual endings are used with close friends, family, or people younger than you. Learning these helps you speak appropriately in different social settings.

examples.english: Hello! How are you feeling today?
Hi! Have you been well?
Thank you. I appreciate your help.

pages.title: Remember vs forget
pages.description: In Korean, 기억하다 means 'to remember' and 잊다 means 'to forget.' When you want someone to remind you of something, you can say 알려 주세요. If you almost forgot some…
pages.imageAlt: Remember vs forget in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused about 기억하다 vs 잊다? 🔴 기억하다 [gieokhada] - to remember
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 기억하다 means 'to remember' and 잊다 means 'to forget.' When you want someone to remind you of something, you can say 알려 주세요. If you almost forgot something, you can say 깜빡할 뻔했어요. These words help you talk about memory and forgetting in daily life.

examples.english: Do you remember the appointment tomorrow?
I forgot something important.
I almost forgot. Please remind me.

pages.title: See / watch / look scenes
pages.titleEn: See / watch / look scenes in Korean
pages.description: These Korean verbs all relate to seeing or watching, but they have different meanings. 보다 means to look at something briefly or generally. 지켜보다 means to watc…
pages.imageAlt: See / watch / look scenes in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How do you say "see" or "watch" in Korean? It depends on the situation! 👀 보다 [boda] - to look at something quickly
pages.explanationEn: These Korean verbs all relate to seeing or watching, but they have different meanings. 보다 means to look at something briefly or generally. 지켜보다 means to watch something carefully for a while. 구경하다 means to sightsee or look around a place. 쳐다보다 means to stare at something, often with focus or surprise.

examples.english: I am looking out the window.

examples.korean: 아이가 놀이터에서 노는 것을 지켜보고 있어요.
examples.english: I am watching the child playing at the playground.
I sightsee famous places in Seoul.

pages.title: Seems / looks like in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, expressions like '것 같아요', '보여요', '들려요', and '느낌이 들어요' are used to say something seems or looks a certain way. They help you share your guesses or…
pages.imageAlt: Seems / looks like in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How do you say "seems like" or "looks like" in Korean? 🔴 것 같아요 [geot gatayo] - seems like
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, expressions like '것 같아요', '보여요', '들려요', and '느낌이 들어요' are used to say something seems or looks a certain way. They help you share your guesses or feelings about what you see, hear, or sense. These phrases are useful for polite conversation when you want to express uncertainty or make a soft statement.

examples.english: It seems like the weather will be good today.
That person looks happy.
I hear the sound of the door closing.

pages.title: Self vs others in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows words used to talk about doing things by yourself or with others in Korean. '스스로' means doing something by yourself, while '서로' means doing…
pages.imageAlt: Self vs others in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Know the difference between self and others in Korean👇 🔴 스스로 [seuseuro] - by myself
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows words used to talk about doing things by yourself or with others in Korean. '스스로' means doing something by yourself, while '서로' means doing something with each other. '혼자' means alone, and '같이' means together. These words help you describe who is involved in an action.

examples.english: I study by myself.
We help each other.
I watch a movie together with a friend.

pages.title: Start & finish the day in Korean
pages.titleEn: Start & finish the day in Korean
pages.description: This chart shows common Korean verbs used to describe starting and finishing your day. You can use these words to talk about waking up, going to work or scho…
pages.imageAlt: Start & finish the day in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: How to start and finish your day in Korean 👇 🔴 일어나다 [ireonada] - wake up
pages.explanationEn: This chart shows common Korean verbs used to describe starting and finishing your day. You can use these words to talk about waking up, going to work or school, coming home, and going to bed. Some verbs have pairs that depend on whether you are talking about work or school. These verbs are useful for daily conversations.

examples.english: I wake up in the morning and go to work.
Students wake up in the morning and go to school.
I come home in the evening and go to bed early.

pages.title: Time words in Korean
pages.description: These Korean time words help you talk about when something happens. '지금' means 'now,' and it's used for the present moment. '아까' refers to a short time ago,…
pages.imageAlt: Time words in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Talk about time in Korean like a pro! 🕒 지금 [jigeum] - now
pages.explanationEn: These Korean time words help you talk about when something happens. '지금' means 'now,' and it's used for the present moment. '아까' refers to a short time ago, like 'a while ago.' '나중에' means 'later,' indicating a future time, and '내일' specifically means 'tomorrow.' Learning these words helps you describe time clearly in everyday conversations.

examples.english: What are you doing now?
I met a friend a while ago.
I will call you again later.

pages.title: Also / too particles in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, particles like 도 (do) and 만 (man) are used to express 'also', 'too', or 'only'. They help add meaning to nouns by showing inclusion or limitation.…
pages.imageAlt: Also / too particles in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Learn how to say "also" or "too" in Korean with these easy examples👇 🔴 나도 [nado] - me too
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, particles like 도 (do) and 만 (man) are used to express 'also', 'too', or 'only'. They help add meaning to nouns by showing inclusion or limitation. For example, 도 means 'also' or 'too', while 만 means 'only'. These particles are important for making comparisons or emphasizing specific items in a sentence.

Understanding the difference helps you choose the right word depending on the situation.

pages.imageAlt: Leave vs Depart in Korean — Korean vocab chart

pages.explanationEn: Both '떠나다' and '출발하다' mean to leave or go away, but they are used differently. '떠나다' is a general term for leaving a place or situation. '출발하다' is more specific and is used when starting a trip, journey, or moving from one place to another, often with a vehicle.

examples.english: I left the house.
The train departs at 9 o'clock.
We prepared to leave for the trip.

pages.title: Like vs Love
pages.description: In Korean, 좋아하다 (joahada) means 'to like' and 사랑하다 (saranghada) means 'to love.' 좋아하다 is used for general liking or fondness, such as liking food, hobbies, o…

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 좋아하다 (joahada) means 'to like' and 사랑하다 (saranghada) means 'to love.' 좋아하다 is used for general liking or fondness, such as liking food, hobbies, or people. 사랑하다 expresses a deeper, more emotional feeling, often used for romantic love or strong affection.

examples.english: I like Korean food.
I love that person.
I like music, but I love my family.

pages.title: Look vs Check

pages.explanationEn: Both '보다' and '확인하다' are verbs related to seeing or checking something in Korean. '보다' means 'to look' or 'to see' and is used when you simply observe or watch something. '확인하다' means 'to check' or 'to confirm' and is used when you want to verify or make sure of something. These verbs help express different ways of using your eyes in daily situations.

examples.english: I watch the news every morning.
Please check your plane ticket again.
Look outside the window. The weather is nice.

pages.title: Make vs Produce
pages.description: Both 만들다 and 제작하다 mean to create something, but 만들다 is more general and commonly used in everyday situations for making or building things. 제작하다 is more form…

pages.intro: 🗣️ When you want to say "to make" something by hand or casually: ➡️ 만들다 [mandeulda] (Make)
pages.explanationEn: Both 만들다 and 제작하다 mean to create something, but 만들다 is more general and commonly used in everyday situations for making or building things. 제작하다 is more formal and often used for producing items like movies, products, or artworks. Use 만들다 for simple making and 제작하다 for professional or official production.

examples.english: I made a cake.
This company produces cars.
The students are making robots.

pages.title: Meet vs Meet (humble)

pages.intro: Need to meet someone casually or respectfully? Use these two verbs👇 🔴 만나다 [mannada] - Meet (general)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, there are different words for "meet" depending on the level of politeness. "만나다 (mannada)" is the standard word used in everyday situations. "뵙다 (boepda)" is the humble form used when speaking about meeting someone of higher status or to show respect. Understanding these helps you speak politely in different social settings.

examples.english: I meet my friend.

Tomorrow, I will meet (humbly) the company president.

pages.title: Need vs Require
pages.description: Both 필요하다 and 요구하다 express the idea of needing something, but they are used differently. 필요하다 means 'to need' in a general or personal sense, like needing an…

pages.explanationEn: Both 필요하다 and 요구하다 express the idea of needing something, but they are used differently. 필요하다 means 'to need' in a general or personal sense, like needing an item or help. 요구하다 means 'to require' or 'to demand,' often used in more formal or official situations. Understanding the difference helps you use these verbs correctly in everyday and formal contexts.

examples.english: I need water.

examples.english: The company requires more effort from the employees.
This work needs a lot of time.

pages.title: Okay / fine vs Good
pages.titleEn: Okay / fine vs Good in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, 괜찮다 (gwaenchanta) and 좋다 (jota) both express positive feelings but are used differently. 괜찮다 means 'okay' or 'fine' and is often used to show some…

pages.intro: When someone asks "How are you?" and you want to say it's okay or good, what's the difference? 🔴 괜찮다 [gwaenchanta] - Okay, fine
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 괜찮다 (gwaenchanta) and 좋다 (jota) both express positive feelings but are used differently. 괜찮다 means 'okay' or 'fine' and is often used to show something is acceptable or not a problem. 좋다 means 'good' and expresses a stronger positive evaluation or preference. Understanding when to use each helps you sound more natural in everyday conversations.

examples.english: Is this food okay?
The weather is good today.
I thought that movie was fine.

pages.title: Open vs Turn on
pages.titleEn: Open vs Turn on in Korean

pages.intro: 🗣️ Real-life Korean vibes: ➡️ Open: 열다 [yeolda] (Open) 📈🔥
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 열다 (yeolda) means to open something like a door, book, or window. 켜다 (kyeoda) means to turn on devices or lights. Both verbs describe actions but are used for different objects and situations.

examples.english: Open the door.
Turn on the light.
I open the book and study.

pages.title: Receive vs Obtain / get

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 받다 and 얻다 mean to get something, but they are used differently. 받다 is used when you receive something from someone, like a gift or a message. 얻다 means to obtain or get something through effort or by finding it. Understanding the difference helps you use these words correctly in daily conversations.

examples.english: I received a book from the teacher.
I obtained information from the internet.
I got a letter from my friend.

pages.title: Rest vs Relax
pages.description: In Korean, 쉬다 and 휴식하다 both relate to taking a break, but they are used differently. 쉬다 means to rest, often implying stopping work or activity to recover en…
pages.imageAlt: Rest vs Relax in Korean — Korean vocab chart

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 쉬다 and 휴식하다 both relate to taking a break, but they are used differently. 쉬다 means to rest, often implying stopping work or activity to recover energy. 휴식하다 means to relax, focusing more on calming the mind and body. Understanding these differences helps you choose the right word in daily conversations.

examples.english: I rested at home after finishing work.
I relax in the park on weekends.

examples.korean: 피곤할 때는 잠깐 쉬는 게 좋아요.

pages.intro: 🗣️ When you want to speak directly: ➡️ 말하다 [malhada] (Say) is your go-to!
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 말하다 and 언급하다 relate to speaking, but they are used differently. 말하다 means 'to say' and is used for general speaking or expressing something directly. 언급하다 means 'to mention' and is used when referring to a topic or bringing something up in conversation. Understanding the difference helps you speak more naturally.

examples.korean: 그는 오늘 아침에 학교에 간다고 말했어요.
examples.english: He said he went to school this morning.
They mentioned the new plan in the meeting.
My friend said my name.

pages.title: See vs Be seen / appear
pages.titleEn: See vs Be seen / appear in Korean
pages.description: In Korean, '보다' means 'to see' and is used when you actively look at something. '보이다' means 'to be seen' or 'to appear,' and it describes something that can…
pages.imageAlt: See vs Be seen / appear in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: 🗣️ Real-life Korean vibes: ➡️ See: 보다 [boda] (See) 📈🔥
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, '보다' means 'to see' and is used when you actively look at something. '보이다' means 'to be seen' or 'to appear,' and it describes something that can be seen or appears to someone. These verbs show the difference between actively seeing and something being visible or appearing.

examples.english: I see the mountain.
The mountain is clearly visible.
That person appears from far away.

pages.title: Send vs Mail / ship
pages.titleEn: Send vs Mail / ship in Korean

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 보내다 means 'to send' and is used for sending things like messages, gifts, or people. 부치다 means 'to mail' or 'to ship' and is used when sending packages or letters through postal services. Both verbs involve sending, but 보내다 is more general, while 부치다 specifically refers to mailing or shipping items.

examples.english: Send a letter to a friend.
Mail a package.
Send a photo by email.

pages.title: Speak / say vs Talk / chat
pages.titleEn: Speak / say vs Talk / chat in Korean

pages.intro: Use these when you want to express speech or conversation 👇 🔴 말하다 [malhada] - Speak / say
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 말하다 and 이야기하다 relate to speaking, but they are used differently. 말하다 means to speak or say something directly, often focusing on the content of what is said. 이야기하다 means to talk or chat, usually implying a more casual or conversational exchange. Understanding these differences helps you choose the right word in daily conversations.

examples.english: The teacher said something important.
I had a fun chat with my friend.
He did not speak about the problem.

pages.title: Speak vs Speak (honorific)

pages.intro: Want to sound polite in Korean? Use these when you talk to elders or bosses 👇 🔴 말하다 [malhada] - Speak (plain)
pages.explanationEn: In Korean, there are different ways to say 'speak' depending on the level of politeness. '말하다' is the standard way to say 'speak' used in casual or neutral situations. '말씀하다' is the honorific form, used to show respect when speaking about someone of higher status or older age. Understanding when to use these forms helps you communicate politely in Korean.

examples.english: I speak when talking with my friend.
Please speak to the teacher (honorific).
Grandmother spoke slowly (honorific).

pages.title: Start vs Begin
pages.description: Both 시작하다 and 개시하다 mean to start or begin something in Korean. 시작하다 is more commonly used in everyday situations and casual speech. 개시하다 is more formal and o…

pages.intro: Use these when you want to talk about starting something new 👇 🔴 시작하다 [sijakhada] - start (everyday use)
pages.explanationEn: Both 시작하다 and 개시하다 mean to start or begin something in Korean. 시작하다 is more commonly used in everyday situations and casual speech. 개시하다 is more formal and often used in official or written contexts. They can often be used interchangeably, but the level of formality is the main difference.

examples.english: To start the class.
To begin the meeting.
The festival starts this afternoon.

pages.title: Study vs Review
pages.description: In Korean, 공부하다 means to study, which is the act of learning new information or skills. 복습하다 means to review, which is going over what you have already learn…

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 공부하다 means to study, which is the act of learning new information or skills. 복습하다 means to review, which is going over what you have already learned to remember it better. Both are important for school and learning, but 공부하다 is for new learning, while 복습하다 is for reinforcing past lessons.

examples.korean: 공부하고 복습하면 더 잘 기억할 수 있어요.
examples.english: If you study and review, you can remember better.

pages.title: Think vs Consider
pages.description: Both '생각하다' and '검토하다' relate to thinking, but they are used differently. '생각하다' means to think or have an idea about something, often in a general way. '검토하…
pages.imageAlt: Think vs Consider in Korean — Korean vocab chart
pages.intro: Confused about when to use 생각하다 vs 검토하다? 🔴 생각하다 [saenggakhada] - to think about something
pages.explanationEn: Both '생각하다' and '검토하다' relate to thinking, but they are used differently. '생각하다' means to think or have an idea about something, often in a general way. '검토하다' means to carefully consider or review something before making a decision. Use '생각하다' for everyday thoughts and '검토하다' for more serious or detailed consideration.

examples.korean: 나는 내일 여행을 갈지 생각하고 있어요.
examples.english: I am thinking about whether to go on a trip tomorrow.
Please carefully review the contract before signing.

examples.korean: 새로운 아이디어를 생각해 보고, 팀과 함께 검토할 거예요.
examples.english: I will think of new ideas and then consider them with the team.

pages.title: Think vs Feel

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 생각하다 means to think or to have an opinion, focusing on mental processes and reasoning. 느끼다 means to feel, referring to emotions or physical sensations. Understanding the difference helps you express thoughts and feelings clearly in Korean.

examples.english: I think the weather is nice today.
When I listen to music, I feel good.
He is thinking deeply about the problem.

pages.title: Tired vs Sleepy
pages.description: In Korean, 피곤하다 means 'tired' and describes feeling physically or mentally exhausted after work or activities. 졸리다 means 'sleepy' and refers to the feeling o…
pages.imageAlt: Tired vs Sleepy in Korean — Korean vocab chart

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, 피곤하다 means 'tired' and describes feeling physically or mentally exhausted after work or activities. 졸리다 means 'sleepy' and refers to the feeling of wanting to sleep or dozing off. Both words relate to low energy but focus on different causes and sensations.

examples.korean: 오늘 하루 종일 일해서 너무 피곤해요.
examples.english: I am very tired because I worked all day today.

examples.korean: 수업 시간에 너무 졸려서 집중하기 어려워요.
examples.english: I am so sleepy during class that it is hard to concentrate.

examples.korean: 운동 후에 피곤하지만 잠이 안 와요.
examples.english: I am tired after exercising, but I can't fall asleep.

pages.title: Use vs Utilize

Understanding when to use each helps you sound more natural in Korean.

examples.english: I use a computer every day.

examples.korean: 이 도구를 잘 활용하면 일이 더 쉬워져요.
examples.english: If you utilize this tool well, the work becomes easier.
Be careful when you use your phone.

pages.title: Wait vs Stand by
pages.titleEn: Wait vs Stand by in Korean

examples.english: I am waiting for my friend.
Please stand by until the plane departs.
Please wait in the waiting room until the doctor comes.

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, both 원하다 and 희망하다 express wanting something, but they have different feelings. 원하다 is used for simple wants or needs, like wanting food or an item. 희망하다 is stronger and more formal, showing a deep desire or hope for something important or future-oriented.

examples.english: I want a new car.
He desires a good job.
We want happiness.

pages.title: Wear (clothes) vs Wear (hat / glasses)
pages.titleEn: Wear (clothes) vs Wear (hat / glasses) in Korean

pages.explanationEn: In Korean, different verbs are used to say 'wear' depending on the item. Use 입다 (ipda) when talking about wearing clothes like shirts or pants. Use 쓰다 (sseuda) when referring to wearing accessories on your head or face, such as hats or glasses. This helps make your Korean more natural and clear.

examples.english: I wore new clothes today.

I wear glasses and read a book.

pages.title: Wear (clothes) vs Wear (shoes)

examples.korean: 추울 때 두꺼운 코트를 입고 부츠를 신어요.
examples.english: When it's cold, I wear a thick coat and boots.
